edits.target: - Example pattern: a clue about a region 'in this country' wants the country, not the region. A clue about 'one of these "watering holes"' wants the real object being nicknamed, not the nickname.
edits.content:
- Example pattern: a clue about a region 'in this country' wants the country, not the region.
- 'ONE OF THESE <noun>' with a generic or quoted noun ('one of these "watering holes"'): the answer is either a specific KIND of that noun or the real object the nickname stands for. Never answer with a word already in the clue or a neighbouring object that merely fits the setting. Look for compounds built on the clue's noun that recur in passage titles near the anchor. Test: for a literal noun, '<answer> is a kind of <clue noun>' must be true; for a quoted nickname, give the real object, not the nickname.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - POSSESSIVE / OWNER clues: when the clue attaches a work, album, song or sub-part to 'he / she / his / her / this <org>'s' ('"X" is the last song on his 1983 album'; 'A & B are in this organization's Hall of Fame, founded in 1967'), the answer is the PERSON or ORGANIZATION that made or owns it, never the work, album or part named in the clue. A title already quoted in the clue is the wrong slot. Test the identifying detail (year, number) against the candidate and choose the body that has it, not a larger related body.

edits.target: Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.
edits.content: - COPY IN FULL: Rule 4's shortening rules (drop qualifiers or articles, singularize, drop descriptors) do NOT apply to a verbatim archive answer. Keep everything it shows (', State' or ', Country', a trailing noun, a plural, a leading 'the'). Strip only contestant text ('. right: Name', 'wrong:') and any 'What is / Who is' wrapper.

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content: - A quoted fragment that starts or ends with '...' asks for the MISSING WORD(S) that complete a famous title, phrase or lyric, NOT the singer, author or work that contains it. Unless a verbatim archive hit (Rule 3) says otherwise, scan passage titles for other items built on the same fragment and give the word that completes the best-known classic title, not the first or most recent hit. Never answer with a performer's name.

edits.target: Other clue details (diet, ingredient, cooking method) are just conditions on the generic dish.
edits.content:
- '<Modifier> version of this <generic noun>': the modifier is only a hint and is NOT part of the answer. Give the bare family name as the passages title it, keeping a plural headword plural.
- SUPERLATIVE / COMPARISON clues ('greater than all other X put together', 'the most', 'the largest'): the answer must beat every other candidate, including earlier or later numbered entities in the passages. If an archive hit is cut off before the answer, use your own knowledge to pick the candidate that makes the comparison true; a later, larger entity that includes the earlier one wins.

edits.target: look for the passage that glosses it ('locally referred to as lambi') and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content:
- DEFINITION / GLOSS clues ('Term for ...', 'This phrase describes ...', 'It's in dictionaries as ...'): the answer is the single TERM being defined. Find the dictionary or encyclopedia passage whose title or headword ('X | Define X', 'X - definition of X') is glossed with the clue's own words. Answer with that headword in the form shown, keeping hyphens and keeping the plural if the clue describes a group. Drop the clue's category noun unless it is part of the standard name, and do not substitute a description or synonym.
- 'N-word' hints ('this 3-word phrase') work like a letter count: the answer must have exactly N words.

edits.target: - Archive lines may also be formatted 'CATEGORY | clue text | answer'. Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - The archive answer and its CATEGORY header beat the slot-type check: a pun or idiom answer is correct even if it does not look like the clue's noun, so do not swap in a literal answer. Stage directions and audio/video links inside an archived clue are noise. The hit may sit in a recap or blog quoting the clue ('The clue: ... "What is X?"'); if the recap marks that response wrong, use the correct answer it gives.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Otherwise (no archive hit), build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details. Use passage TITLES ([TLE] headers) and first lines as evidence: the entity recurring across several titles or snippets together with the clue's distinctive details (place, year, number, sport, institution) is usually the answer, and a clue sentence nearly copied inside a passage points to that passage's subject. Commit once it fits every detail.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content: - 'X seen here / shown here is used with this <category>' (picture missing): the clue names an object and asks for its standard partner. Search the passages for the object word next to a candidate of the stated category and answer with the bare partner word, not the object word and not a looser category member that never appears paired with the object.

edits.target: - For nickname clues about a person ('known as "Uncle Walter"'), answer with the real name as it appears in the context (Walter Cronkite), not the nickname. Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - A quoted epithet, tagline or billing that recurs word-for-word across many passages labels ONE subject (fictional characters too). Answer with the name that sits next to that phrase in most passage titles and snippets, not the epithet, a word from it, or the author.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Species / official-symbol clues ('this bird on the state seal'): when the passages consistently give a qualified standard common name, keep the qualifier, since it is part of the species name. Do not shorten to the bare genus word and do not add 'state bird'.
